title: Measure powdered formula into a 4-ounce bottle: two unpacked scoops, each leveled against the tin's leveling bar
instruction: Measure the formula into this bottle.
context: Childcare workers and nannies (O*NET 39-9011.00), home health aides and parents measure powdered infant formula into bottles many times a day. US standard formulas are mixed at one unpacked, level scoop of powder per 2 fl oz of water (Similac's preparation directions), so the 4 fl oz of water already in this bottle takes exactly two level scoops. A scoop dipped into the powder comes out heaped, and a heaped scoop holds about 29% more powder than a level one; pressing the powder down adds more. The CDC's formula guidance says to use the exact amounts on the container because adding too much or too little formula can make a baby sick, and powder stirred into water cannot be taken back out. The skill is the physical measuring: dip, draw the scoop up against the tin's leveling bar so the heap falls back into the tin, tip it into the bottle's neck, twice, without packing it or spilling; capping and shaking the bottle come after and are not part of this task.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. All objects are fixed except the scoop. A white steel formula tin, 14.6 cm across and 10 cm tall with a plain pale-blue label band, lid off, stands with its axis at x 31, y 11; it holds 700 g of pale cream powder (0.50 g/mL loose) whose top is about 0.65 cm below the rim. A rigid gray leveling bar 1 cm wide and 0.4 cm thick is fixed across the opening along x, its center line at y 12.5, its underside at the rim (10 cm). A clear 270 mL wide-neck plastic bottle, 6 cm across and 11.5 cm tall to the top of its neck (5 cm opening), stands in a gray holder ring 9 cm across at x 40, y -3; it holds 120 mL (4 fl oz) of water with the 120 mL line marked. A dark-blue plastic scoop (45 g with a weighted handle) lies on a white scoop stand at x 23, y -12.5: its round handle, 2.5 cm across and 7 cm long, runs along y with its center at y -12.5, 8 cm up, resting on a post 1.6 cm wide; a neck runs down from the handle's +y end to a round bowl 3.9 cm across outside (3.6 cm inside, 1.75 cm deep, 17.8 mL) whose center is at y -4.75, resting on a 3.5 cm square pad 2.2 cm tall. A level scoop of this powder weighs 8.9 g, close to the 8.6 to 8.8 g on US labels.
scoring: A correct feed is two level scoops, 17.8 g, each leveled against the bar: the trial scores 0 if any scoopful reaches the bottle without the bar having passed over all of the scoop's mouth, at its underside, since that scoopful was dipped (tipping the scoop to shed its heap, or carrying it over the bar's top, does not level it). The trial also scores 0 once the bottle has held more than 19.1 g (17.8 g plus 7%), however it got there, since powder in water cannot be removed: one heaped scoop with one level is up to 20.3 g (part of a heap can fall off on the way, and the sim's run of it ended at 19.0 g, inside the window, so the strike-off rule is what catches it), two heaped 22.9 g, scoops pressed down 20 g or more, three level scoops 26.5 g. Otherwise it scores 0 while a tool point is within 4 cm of the scoop's handle, neck or bowl (still holding it), while the scoop is still moving or has fallen off the table, or with 1 g or more of powder on the table. Then, weighing the powder in the bottle at the end (the result must hold 1 s): 1.0 for 16.6 to 19.1 g in the bottle (plus or minus 7%: a scoop drawn 1 mm short of the bar's underside keeps about 0.5 g more) with both arms back home and still (each tool point within 3 cm of where it started); 0.9 for the same with the arms not home; 0.25 for 8.3 to 9.5 g, exactly one level scoop with nothing over (half done); 0 for any other amount, including doing nothing. The grams above use the sim's nominal level scoop, 8.9 g (US labels give 8.6 to 8.8 g). In a real build the windows come from the tin actually used: weigh 10 level scoops of that product, each leveled against the bar, take their mean m, and score 2m plus or minus 7% for 1.0 and m plus or minus 7% for 0.25, with the over-strong latch at 2m plus 7%; 7% is the 1 mm leveling error and stays wider than the scatter of hand-leveled scoops (check that the 10 weighings fall within plus or minus 3% of m). Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.9 and 1.0. In a real trial, weigh the bottle on a 0.1 g kitchen scale before and after, weigh any powder brushed off the table, and check on the video that each scoop was drawn along the bar before it went to the bottle.
reset_notes: Pour out the bottle and refill it with 120 mL of water; top the tin back up to 700 g and smooth the surface; lay the scoop back on its stand, clean and dry. Powder in the bottle is consumed. Before the first trial with a new tin or lot, recalibrate the gram windows from 10 weighed level scoops (see scoring).
fidelity: The powder is a scored bulk model, not particles: densities (loose 0.50 g/mL, packed 0.64), heaps at a 42 degree angle of repose, dips, the strike-off under the bar, pours and spills move grams from the poses each step. The powder has no weight or collision, so a tipped scoop would shed its heap exactly; the scorer therefore requires the bar. Powder standing above the scoop's rim is drawn orange so heaped and level read apart on camera; stirring the bottle is not modeled.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0 (2,400 steps); demo: 1.0 (1,271 steps, 18.1 g in the bottle). Mistake variants in the sim: do nothing 0, two heaped scoops 0, one heaped and one level 0 (18.99 g, caught by the strike-off rule), one level scoop 0.25, three level scoops 0.
